passage: Imagine that you are asked to tap out the rhythm of a well-known song, such as a birthday song, on a table while a listener tries to guess the tune. In a famous experiment at Stanford University, the tappers predicted that listeners would name the song about half of the time. In reality, listeners guessed correctly in only about two and a half percent of the cases. The tappers, who could hear the melody in their heads, found it impossible to {1|imagine} the taps as a meaningless series of knocks. Psychologists call this problem the curse of knowledge: once we know something, we find it very hard to remember what it was like not to know it. The curse appears wherever expertise meets inexperience. A teacher who has taught a subject for many years may skip steps that seem {2|obvious}, leaving students confused. A programmer writes instructions that only another programmer can follow, and a doctor uses words that patients do not understand. Because the knowledge is stored so deeply, experts are often unaware that they are leaving anything out. Fortunately, the curse can be {3|worsened} by simple habits. Asking a beginner to explain the idea back in his or her own words reveals gaps that the expert cannot see. Using concrete examples and everyday comparisons, and testing a draft on a newcomer before presenting it, also helps. The best explainers are not those who know the most. They are those who can still recall the {4|struggle} of learning and who are willing to {5|adjust} their words to the person in front of them.

Why Beginners Should Never Learn from Experts
